idiom_name: session-scoped keyed registry (identity key -> instance) consulted by every finder
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the session/unit of work owns a map keyed on the persistent identity (entity type plus primary key). Every finder consults the map first, queries the store only on a miss, and registers the object it materialises; from then on the map - not the database - decides which instance the session sees. Keep the map's lifetime identical to the session's, key only on stable identity, and decide up front whether the map owns objects (strong references) or merely indexes them (weak references), because that choice fixes when an instance may be re-materialised.
code_sketch:
find(id):
    key = (entity_type, id)
    if key in session.identity_map:
        return session.identity_map[key]     # no SQL on hit
    obj = mapper.load(id)                    # SQL only on miss
    session.identity_map[key] = obj          # register for later lookups
    return obj
# session end: discard the map; the next session starts empty
pitfalls: Registering only in the loader: any path that constructs an object directly (deserialisation, DTO copy, raw query) forks identity - every load path must consult and register.
Keying on mutable attributes or on object identity instead of the persistent identity: rows with changed keys become duplicates.
Scoping the map globally instead of per session: rows stay alive (memory) and stale (correctness) beyond the unit of work.

Scoping the map globally instead of per session: rows stay alive (memory) and stale (correctness) beyond the unit of work.

Stale data after concurrent updates: if one transaction modifies a row and a second transaction re-reads that row within a session that already cached it, the second read returns the cached (old) instance. Use explicit refresh/expire or populate_existing when the latest database state is required.

FOR UPDATE queries returning cached (stale) data: when an entity is already in the identity map, a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE still returns the cached instance, not the freshly locked row. Use populate_existing() or expire() before the locking query to force a re-fetch.

Long-running sessions and batch jobs: the identity map grows without bound as more rows are loaded, eventually causing OutOfMemoryError. Use periodic flush-and-clear cycles or StatelessSession for bulk operations that do not need identity guarantees.

Reference semantics confusion in multi-DbContext workflows: creating a new DbContext (or session) per service call means each context has its own identity map and its own instance for the same row. This can silently produce divergent copies when one service creates entities and another reads them in a different context.

Weak-reference GC pressure: in SQLAlchemy, the identity map uses WeakInstanceDict — dereferenced objects are garbage-collected even while the session is open, causing unexpected re-loads from the database in long-lived sessions.

Deserialised graphs with duplicate instances: loading a JSON or external graph that contains multiple references to the same entity (same primary key) creates multiple instances unless identity resolution is applied on deserialisation. ORMs throw on attempted re-attachment of a duplicate; use TrackGraph with explicit deduplication for EF Core or equivalent merge/attach hooks for other frameworks.

Wrong move: sharing one identity map across requests or tenants -> stale objects, memory retention, and cross-request data leakage -> instead scope it to a request or unit of work and clear or discard it at the boundary.

Wrong move: treating the map as a general query/result cache for non-primary-key filters -> the identity map is not consulted and fresh query results are still required -> instead use an explicit query or second-level cache while keeping identity resolution session-scoped.

Wrong move: attaching a deserialised graph with duplicate instances directly to a tracked context -> duplicate-key tracking errors or divergent copies -> instead deduplicate by identity and merge or attach through the context's identity-resolution API.
